nodes.label: The Hilly Flanks Neolithic
nodes.full: The farming and herding package — domesticated wheat, barley, sheep and goat — put together in the well-watered foothills of the Zagros and Taurus in the pre-pottery Neolithic, and carried down onto the Mesopotamian plain by its first villagers.
nodes.src: background — Robert Braidwood's Jarmo project (1948–55); Frank Hole's Deh Luran work.

nodes.label: The wider Halaf world
nodes.full: The Halaf culture reached across northern Syria and into southeast Anatolia; its painted pottery, tholoi and exchange networks tied together a dispersed, non-hierarchical north of which the Iraqi sites are the eastern edge.
nodes.src: background — Akkermans & Schwartz, 'The Archaeology of Syria' (2003); Stuart Campbell.

nodes.label: The Arabian Neolithic of the Gulf
nodes.full: The herding, fishing and pearling communities of the Gulf coast — Dalma, Marawah, as-Sabiyah — that took in Ubaid pottery and, on the southern reading, sent back fish, pearl-shell and dates. See the folio gulf-prehistory-8000bc-3000bc.
nodes.src: background — Robert Carter on Gulf Ubaid contact; see gulf-prehistory-8000bc-3000bc.

nodes.label: The Uruk period
nodes.full: The centuries after 3800 BC when the southern towns became the world's first cities — mass society, monumental temples, the cylinder seal, and the invention of writing. The Ubaid towns grow into it with no break in occupation.
nodes.src: background — see the folio uruk-3800bc-2900bc; Hans Nissen, 'The Early History of the Ancient Near East' (1988).

nodes.label: Hassuna — the first villages of the northern plain
nodes.full: On the rain-fed steppe of the upper Tigris and the Sinjar plain, the earliest fully agricultural villages of Mesopotamia formed — small clusters of rectangular multi-room mudbrick houses with courtyards, grain bins and bread ovens, farming barley and emmer and herding sheep and goats. The specialised onager-hunting outpost at Umm Dabaghiyah shows the range of the economy. Coarse cooking pots and simple painted or incised wares mark the horizon.
nodes.src: Type site excavated by Seton Lloyd & Fuad Safar for the Iraqi Directorate of Antiquities, 'Tell Hassuna' (1945, JNES); Umm Dabaghiyah by Diana Kirkbride (1971–75); Yarim Tepe I by the Soviet expedition of Merpert & Munchaev.

nodes.label: Samarra — farming crosses the dry line
nodes.full: Along the middle Tigris, at the edge of where rain-fed farming is possible, Samarran communities pushed agriculture into drier land by cutting simple canals from the river — the first irrigation in Mesopotamia. Tell es-Sawwan was a substantial planted village with T-shaped houses, alabaster figurines and statuettes in its graves, and a defensive ditch. Its fine painted pottery, with dancing women, fish and scorpions swirling around the interior, was carried far beyond the Samarra zone.
nodes.src: Pottery first recognised by Ernst Herzfeld at Samarra (1911–13); Tell es-Sawwan excavated by the Iraqi Directorate of Antiquities (El-Wailly & Abu es-Soof, 1964–71); Choga Mami by Joan Oates (1967–68), who defined the 'Samarra' irrigation model.

nodes.label: Halaf — the painted-pottery north
nodes.full: Across northern Mesopotamia and into Syria and southeast Anatolia, Halaf communities lived in villages of round domed houses (tholoi) and produced the most technically and artistically accomplished painted pottery of the ancient Near East — thin-walled, lustrous, polychrome, and traded as a prestige good over hundreds of kilometres. No site dominates the others and no palaces or central stores appear: the Halaf north looks like a network of roughly equal communities, not a hierarchy.
nodes.src: Tell Halaf excavated by Max von Oppenheim (1911–13, 1927–29); Arpachiyah by Max Mallowan & J. C. Rose (1933); modern synthesis in Stuart Campbell and in Akkermans & Schwartz, 'The Archaeology of Syria' (2003).

nodes.label: The first settlement of the southern marshes
nodes.full: At the head of the Gulf, on levees and turtlebacks amid the marshes, the earliest known settlers of the southern alluvium built small villages with painted pottery close in style to Samarra's. Eridu's deepest levels begin a temple sequence rebuilt on the same spot for two thousand years; Tell el-Oueili has the oldest alluvial deposits yet found. Whether earlier villages lie buried under metres of river silt and a risen water table is the unanswered 'Ubaid problem'.
nodes.src: Eridu excavated by Fuad Safar, Seton Lloyd & Mohammad Ali Mustafa (1946–49), published as 'Eridu' (1981); Tell el-Oueili by the French mission under Jean-Louis Huot (1976–89).

nodes.label: The mature Ubaid of the south
nodes.full: The southern culture that gives the whole period its name spread across the alluvium — Ur, Uruk, al-Ubaid, Tell el-Oueili — with a recurring package: the tripartite house and temple plan, greenish painted pottery giving way to plain mass-produced bowls, the bent clay 'sickle' of fired earth, and a slow but steady growth in the number and size of settlements. Society shows differences of wealth and role but no kings and no walled centres.
nodes.src: Al-Ubaid excavated by H. R. Hall & Leonard Woolley (1919, 1923–24); the 'Ubaid' as a period defined at the 1930 Baghdad conference; synthesis in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010).

nodes.label: The first pan-Mesopotamian horizon
nodes.full: Ubaid pottery, the tripartite building and the stamp seal spread north over the former Halaf zone — Tepe Gawra, Tell Zeidan on the Euphrates, sites in the Khabur and up to the Taurus — and down the Arabian shore of the Gulf. For the first time a single material culture linked the whole of Mesopotamia, north and south, and its edges. Whether this was migration, emulation or trade is still argued; the result was a shared world.
nodes.src: Tepe Gawra excavated by E. A. Speiser & Charles Bache (1927–38); Tell Zeidan by Gil Stein (2008–11); the expansion debated across the essays in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010).

nodes.label: The temple towns and the eve of the city
nodes.full: By the end of the period the largest southern sites were true towns of ten hectares or more — Eridu with its mudbrick platform temple, Tell Abada in the Hamrin with its big central house, Kheit Qasim. A two-tier pattern of larger and smaller settlements appears, and the temple stands out as the community's monumental focus. The shift into the Uruk period that follows is gradual, with no break in occupation at the main sites.
nodes.src: Eridu Temple sequence in Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 'Eridu' (1981); Tell Abada by Sabah Abboud Jasim, 'The Ubaid Period in Iraq' (1985); regional synthesis in Susan Pollock, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1999).

nodes.label: The ditch and wall of Tell es-Sawwan
nodes.full: The Samarran village of Tell es-Sawwan was ringed by a ditch three metres deep cut into virgin soil and, on the river side, a buttressed mudbrick wall — the earliest defensive circuit known in Mesopotamia. Whether it guarded stored grain and irrigated land against raiders, or against the Tigris in flood, is disputed; either way it marks a community with something worth enclosing.
nodes.src: Iraqi Directorate of Antiquities excavations (El-Wailly & Abu es-Soof, 'Excavations at Tell es-Sawwan', Sumer 1965); defensive interpretation reviewed in Roger Matthews, 'The Archaeology of Mesopotamia' (2003).

nodes.label: Burnt houses in the Hassuna–Halaf north
nodes.full: Several northern villages preserve houses destroyed by fierce fires — most famously the 'Burnt Village' at Tell Sabi Abyad on the Balikh, whose blaze baked and preserved a store of clay sealings. Whether such fires were accidents, ritual closings or the marks of raiding cannot usually be told, but they show that village life was not without violent episodes.
nodes.src: Yarim Tepe fire levels in Merpert & Munchaev's reports; the Sabi Abyad 'Burnt Village' in Peter Akkermans (ed.), 'Tell Sabi Abyad' (1996) and Akkermans & Duistermaat on its sealings.

nodes.label: The near-absence of war from Ubaid life
nodes.full: Set against the later Uruk and Early Dynastic record — bound prisoners, smiting scenes, city walls, standing armies — Ubaid material culture is strikingly unmartial. Maces and clay sling-bullets occur, but fortified sites are rare and there is no iconography of battle or captives. Many archaeologists read this, with the shallow gradient of Ubaid wealth and status, as a society not yet organised for war.
nodes.src: Argument developed in Gil Stein, 'Economy, Ritual, and Power in Ubaid Mesopotamia' (1994) and in the settlement analyses collected in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010).

nodes.label: Choga Mami and the contested edge of irrigation
nodes.full: On the Mandali fan, where canal farming met the Zagros piedmont and its herding populations, the Samarran site of Choga Mami was entered through a buttressed gateway tower and lay beside some of the oldest traceable irrigation channels in the world. The combination — new canals, new land, a guarded entrance — hints at friction along the frontier between farmers and their neighbours.
nodes.src: Choga Mami excavated by Joan Oates (1967–68), 'Choga Mami 1967–68: A Preliminary Report' (Iraq 1969); irrigation channels discussed in Oates & Oates, 'The Rise of Civilization' (1976).

nodes.label: The clay token accounts
nodes.full: From the earliest villages, small geometric clay objects — cones, spheres, disks, tetrahedra — were shaped, kept and discarded in ones and tens. On the widely held reading they were counters: one token stood for one measure of grain, one jar of oil, one head of livestock, tallied and stored to record a transaction or an obligation. The system is the direct ancestor of the impressed numerals and then the pictographs of Uruk.
nodes.src: Denise Schmandt-Besserat, 'Before Writing' (1992), building on tokens from Jarmo, Tepe Gawra and dozens of other sites; the token-to-writing thesis is qualified by critics (Zimansky 1993; Englund) but the counting function is not disputed.

nodes.label: The stamp seal and the sealed store
nodes.full: Halaf and Ubaid communities carried small stamp seals cut with geometric or animal designs and pressed them into wet clay that closed jars, baskets, sacks and storeroom doors. A broken sealing proved a container had been opened. The 'Burnt Village' at Tell Sabi Abyad preserved some three hundred such sealings from a single destroyed store — the earliest picture of goods moving under an accountable system.
nodes.src: Tepe Gawra glyptic in Speiser & Tobler, 'Excavations at Tepe Gawra' I–II (1935–50); the Sabi Abyad sealing archive in Akkermans & Duistermaat, 'Of Storage and Nomads' (1997).

nodes.label: The temple as a store and a centre
nodes.full: By the late Ubaid the temple at Eridu was the community's one monumental building — a buttressed hall on a platform, with an offering table and thick ash deposits from burnt fish offerings. Many read it as an institution that gathered and redistributed surplus, the germ of the later Sumerian temple estate. Others caution that the physical evidence for large-scale Ubaid redistribution is in fact slight, and the temple may have been mainly a ritual focus.
nodes.src: Eridu temple sequence in Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 'Eridu' (1981); the redistribution debate in Gil Stein, 'Economy, Ritual, and Power in Ubaid Mesopotamia' (1994).

nodes.label: The standardised ration bowl
nodes.full: As Ubaid pottery lost its painted decoration it gained something else: plain, coarse bowls made fast and in bulk to a roughly repeatable size. The usual explanation is that they measured out allocations — of barley, or of the barley beer that was a wage — to people working for a household or temple. The practice hardens into the mass-produced bevelled-rim bowl of the Uruk period that follows.
nodes.src: Discussed in Susan Pollock, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1999), ch. 4; the continuity with Uruk ration bowls in Hans Nissen, 'The Early History of the Ancient Near East' (1988).

nodes.label: The Eridu temple sequence
nodes.full: Under the ziggurat of Ur's age, excavators found some eighteen temples stacked one on another at Eridu, each built on the levelled ruin of the last — from a mud-brick room barely three metres square to a buttressed, tripartite sanctuary raised on a platform. This is the physical root of the ziggurat. Sumerian tradition remembered Eridu as the first city, the home of the wisdom-god Enki, and the place where kingship first came down from heaven.
nodes.src: Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 'Eridu' (1981); the mythological memory in the Sumerian King List and the poem 'Eridu Genesis' (Jacobsen, 1981).

nodes.label: The ophidian figurines of the south
nodes.full: Southern Ubaid graves and houses yield slender clay figures with narrow shoulders, elongated 'lizard' heads, slit coffee-bean eyes and small pellets of clay applied over the body and head. Some are female and cradle infants; some are male. Painted lines may show tattoos or scarification, and the head shapes echo the real cranial modelling practised on Ubaid skulls. What they represent — gods, ancestors, mourners — is unknown.
nodes.src: Ur figurines published by Leonard Woolley; typology in Peter Ucko, 'Anthropomorphic Figurines' (1968); recent discussion in Karina Croucher, 'Death and Dying in the Neolithic Near East' (2012).

nodes.label: The seated female figurines of the Halaf north
nodes.full: Northern Halaf sites produce small seated clay figures of women, sometimes painted, hands beneath the breasts, the body rendered heavy. Long labelled 'mother goddesses' and read as evidence of a fertility cult, they are now treated more carefully — as household objects whose meaning is not recoverable, part of a figurine tradition running back through the earlier Neolithic.
nodes.src: Mallowan & Rose, 'Excavations at Tall Arpachiyah' (Iraq 1935); the cautious re-reading in Douglass Bailey, 'Prehistoric Figurines' (2005).

nodes.label: The cemetery of Eridu
nodes.full: Beside the terminal-Ubaid town lay a formal cemetery of nearly a thousand graves — bodies laid out full length in mud-brick cists, wrapped in matting, provided with painted pots, tools and food, and in a few cases accompanied by a dog laid at the feet. It is one of the earliest large organised burial grounds in Mesopotamia, and the grave goods are modest and fairly even, with only slight differences of wealth.
nodes.src: Published in Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 'Eridu' (1981); mortuary analysis in Jane Moon and in Croucher, 'Death and Dying in the Neolithic Near East' (2012).

nodes.label: Infants beneath the house floor
nodes.full: At Tell es-Sawwan, Yarim Tepe and Ubaid settlements alike, infants and young children were buried in pottery jars set into the floors of lived-in houses, sometimes with beads or a small vessel. Adults were more often taken to a cemetery outside the village. Keeping the youngest dead within the walls tied them to the household and its continuity.
nodes.src: Tell es-Sawwan sub-floor jar burials in the Directorate of Antiquities reports (Sumer 1964–71); the pattern surveyed in Roger Matthews, 'The Archaeology of Mesopotamia' (2003).

nodes.label: The Samarra style
nodes.full: Samarran potters covered the inside of open bowls with dark paint on a buff ground in tight rotating compositions — long-haired women swinging around a central whirl, files of fish, scorpions, birds and antelope, so arranged that the design turns as the bowl turns. It is the first sustained figurative art of Mesopotamia, and its regular layout points to a turning device under the vessel as it was painted.
nodes.src: Ernst Herzfeld, 'Die vorgeschichtlichen Töpfereien von Samarra' (1930); design analysis in Joan Oates, 'The Baked Clay Figurines from Tell es-Sawwan' and in Peter Roger Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The Halaf style and the potter's workshop
nodes.full: Halaf fine ware — thin, hard, burnished, painted in red, black and white on a cream slip with bukrania, rosettes, cross-hatching and stipple — is the technical summit of prehistoric Near Eastern pottery. At Arpachiyah a burned building held unfinished vessels, pigments and tools: a specialist workshop making prestige pots that then travelled hundreds of kilometres as gifts and exchange.
nodes.src: Mallowan & Rose, 'Excavations at Tall Arpachiyah, 1933' (Iraq 1935); production and distribution in Stuart Campbell, 'Rethinking Halaf Chronologies' (2007).

nodes.label: Ubaid ware and the turn to plain
nodes.full: Early Ubaid pottery is greenish buff with loose bands and swags of paint; over the period the painting thins and then largely stops, and the shapes settle into a small repertoire of plain, fast-made bowls and jars. The change is not a loss of skill but a change of purpose — from vessels made for display and the grave to vessels made in quantity for daily allocation and use.
nodes.src: Joan Oates, 'Ur and Eridu, the Prehistory' (Iraq 1960); the functional reading in Susan Pollock, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1999).

nodes.label: The tripartite plan
nodes.full: From the T-shaped houses of Tell es-Sawwan through the Ubaid, a single architectural idea recurs across Mesopotamia: a long central hall, sometimes cruciform, flanked by symmetrical rows of smaller rooms. The same grammar served the largest house in a village and the temple on its platform, scaled up or down. It is the ancestor of the Mesopotamian temple plan of historic times.
nodes.src: Sabah Abboud Jasim, 'The Ubaid Period in Iraq' (1985) on Tell Abada; architectural analysis in Jean-Daniel Forest, 'Mesopotamia: The First Temples' and in Michael Roaf, 'Cultural Atlas of Mesopotamia' (1990).

nodes.label: Labrets, obsidian and the beads of the network
nodes.full: People marked their bodies with lip-plugs and labrets of stone and clay, wore beads of carnelian, obsidian, and shell carried up from the Gulf, and used polished obsidian for mirrors and ornaments. Small pigment palettes and grinders show the working of cosmetics. The materials trace the same long-distance webs that moved pottery and tools.
nodes.src: Yarim Tepe adornment in Merpert & Munchaev, 'The Earliest Evidence for Metallurgy' and site reports; materials surveyed in Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The scant traces of music and dance
nodes.full: Direct evidence is thin: a few bone tubes that may be pipes, fired-clay rattles with pellets inside, and the ring of dancers painted around the Samarra bowls. Taken together with the wider Neolithic Near Eastern record of line-dance imagery, they suggest that communal music and dance were part of village ritual life, even though no instrument survives complete.
nodes.src: Dance imagery discussed in Yosef Garfinkel, 'Dancing at the Dawn of Agriculture' (2003); clay rattles and possible pipes catalogued in site reports from Yarim Tepe and Tepe Gawra.

nodes.label: Standard measures and the share of water
nodes.full: Canal irrigation forces quantitative thinking: a shared channel must be dug and cleared by agreed labour and its water divided by agreed shares, and a store that issues rations must measure them. The uniform ration bowl and the token counts are the visible residue of a society learning to fix, hold and enforce standard amounts — the mental groundwork on which Uruk accounting is built.
nodes.src: Argument in Hans Nissen, Peter Damerow & Robert Englund, 'Archaic Bookkeeping' (1993), reading back from the Uruk texts; irrigation-labour organisation in Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981).

nodes.label: Building on the same ground
nodes.full: At Eridu each temple was raised precisely on the levelled remains of the one before, for some two thousand years. To rebuild that way is to hold a conception of inherited place and continuous obligation — the current community as one link in a line reaching back to the founders. The same instinct keeps ancestors buried under house floors and, later, makes genealogy the language of Mesopotamian legitimacy.
nodes.src: Stratigraphy in Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 'Eridu' (1981); the interpretation of 'genealogies of buildings' in Jean-Daniel Forest and in Roger Matthews, 'The Archaeology of Mesopotamia' (2003).

nodes.label: Anticipating the flood
nodes.full: The rivers of Mesopotamia flood in spring, after the grain is nearly ripe and at the wrong time for sowing — the opposite of the Nile. Farming the alluvium meant learning to predict the rise, bank against it, and store water for the summer crop. No records survive from this period, but the successful spread of irrigation agriculture is itself evidence of close, transmitted attention to the seasonal sky and the river gauge.
nodes.src: The hydrological problem set out in Thorkild Jacobsen, 'Salinity and Irrigation Agriculture in Antiquity' (1982) and Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); no direct Ubaid-period records exist.

nodes.label: The dry-farming north and the irrigated south
nodes.full: North of a line running roughly through Sinjar and the Diyala, enough winter rain falls to grow barley and wheat without irrigation, and the Hassuna and Halaf villages did. South of it — the Samarra zone and the whole alluvium — rain is too little and too unreliable, and farming meant cutting channels from the rivers. This division between a dry-farming north and an irrigating south is the oldest structural fact of Mesopotamian history.
nodes.src: The rainfall boundary mapped in Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); the two farming regimes contrasted in Hans Nissen, 'The Early History of the Ancient Near East' (1988).

nodes.label: Barley, the date palm, the flock and the marsh
nodes.full: The south assembled a rich and storable food economy from unpromising ground: salt-tolerant irrigated barley; the date palm, which gave sugar, wood, fibre and shade and could be grown between the fields; sheep, goats and cattle grazed on the stubble and the marsh margins; and fish, fowl, turtles and reeds taken from the marshes themselves. The combination fed a denser population than the dry-farmed north could.
nodes.src: Reconstruction in Daniel Potts, 'Mesopotamian Civilization: The Material Foundations' (1997); date-palm cultivation in Naomi Miller's archaeobotanical work; marsh economy in the Eridu and al-Ubaid faunal reports.

nodes.label: Wool, milk and the plough animal
nodes.full: Over this period herders began to keep sheep to older ages for their wool, milk cattle and goats, and put oxen to the sledge and the ard. Getting a second, renewable yield from live animals — the 'secondary products' — multiplied what a flock was worth, gave the south its great textile raw material, and made animal traction available for ploughing and hauling.
nodes.src: Andrew Sherratt, 'Plough and Pastoralism: Aspects of the Secondary Products Revolution' (1981); the timing refined for the Near East by Haskel Greenfield and by kill-off patterns in the Tepe Gawra and Yarim Tepe faunal data.

nodes.label: Craft moves out of the household
nodes.full: The finest Halaf pottery came from dedicated workshops, and the plain Ubaid bowls were turned out fast and in bulk — both signs that some production had left the ordinary household for the hands of part- or full-time specialists working for exchange or for an institution. The division of labour that a city runs on has its start here.
nodes.src: Arpachiyah workshop in Mallowan & Rose (1935); specialisation argued in Gil Stein, 'Economy, Ritual, and Power in Ubaid Mesopotamia' (1994) and in Roux & Courty's studies of Ubaid ceramic technique.

nodes.label: The fired-clay sickle
nodes.full: With almost no flint or good stone in the alluvium, southern harvesters used sickle blades of clay fired so hard they cut grain and could be resharpened, then thrown away and replaced. Made in quantity and found in their thousands, the clay sickle let a treeless, stoneless land reap at the scale its irrigated fields demanded — an elegant answer to a shortage that would otherwise have needed constant imports.
nodes.src: Nancy Benco, 'Manufacture and Use of Clay Sickles from the Uruk Mound, Abu Salabikh' (1992); earlier Ubaid examples in the Ur and Eridu material, discussed in Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The grain bin and the held surplus
nodes.full: Samarran and Ubaid houses had built-in bins and separate storerooms, some large enough to hold well over a household's yearly grain. The ability to carry a surplus from one harvest across the year — and across a bad year — is what lets a population grow past subsistence, frees some hands for craft, and gives a store-keeping institution its leverage.
nodes.src: Storage capacity at Tell es-Sawwan and Choga Mami in Joan Oates's reports; the household-store analysis at Tell Abada in Sabah Abboud Jasim, 'The Ubaid Period in Iraq' (1985).

nodes.label: The irrigation canal
nodes.full: At Choga Mami and Tell es-Sawwan, excavators traced some of the oldest artificial watercourses in the world — gravity-fed channels leading river water onto fields beyond the reach of rain. Over the Ubaid period these grew into branching networks. Nothing else the region invented mattered as much: the canal made the southern plain farmable, and everything built there afterwards rests on it.
nodes.src: Joan Oates, 'Choga Mami, 1967–68' (Iraq 1969); the developmental sequence in Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981) and Robert Wenke's survey work.

nodes.label: The slow potter's wheel
nodes.full: A pivoted disc that a potter could spin by hand — the tournette — appears in the Ubaid south. It was not yet the fast kick-wheel, but it let a worker true and finish a vessel while it turned, speeding output and standardising form. It is the first step of a technology that the following Uruk period would push to full mechanised throwing.
nodes.src: Technique reconstructed from wear and manufacturing traces by Valentine Roux & Marie-Agnès Courty; contextualised in Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The two-chamber kiln
nodes.full: Halaf potters fired their fine ware in updraft kilns that separated the fire chamber below from the pottery chamber above, giving the high, even, controllable heat that thin lustrous painted vessels need. The same mastery of contained high temperature underlies the period's early experiments with smelting copper.
nodes.src: Kilns excavated at Yarim Tepe by Merpert & Munchaev; pyrotechnology surveyed in Moorey (1994) and in Thilo Rehren's archaeometallurgical studies of the northern sites.

nodes.label: The moulded mudbrick and the buttress
nodes.full: In a land with no building stone and little timber, Mesopotamians built with mud: rectangular sun-dried bricks shaped in wooden moulds to a repeatable size, laid in mortar, and strengthened by regularly spaced buttresses and recesses that also became the region's monumental style. The Eridu temples and the big Ubaid houses are all built this way.
nodes.src: Brick formats and wall technique in Olivier Aurenche, 'La maison orientale' (1981); the Eridu temple construction in Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 'Eridu' (1981).

nodes.label: The first smelted copper
nodes.full: Small copper items — awls, pins, beads, a few cast pieces — appear at northern sites from the Hassuna–Halaf period, and Yarim Tepe yielded crucible fragments, slag and copper minerals that point to actual smelting, not just the hammering of native metal. Production stayed tiny and ornamental for millennia, but the knowledge was there early.
nodes.src: Merpert & Munchaev on the Yarim Tepe metallurgical finds; the early-smelting claim assessed in Thilo Rehren et al. and in Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The bitumen boat and the earliest sail
nodes.full: A baked-clay boat model from Eridu has a socket amidships for a mast and holes for stays — the oldest evidence anywhere for the sail. Real craft were bundles of reeds sewn together and coated with river bitumen to make them watertight; slabs of that bitumen impressed with reed and barnacle marks have been dug from Ubaid sites on the Gulf coast. These boats moved goods along the rivers and out onto the sea.
nodes.src: Eridu model published in Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 'Eridu' (1981); bitumen boat-slabs and the sailing claim in Robert Carter, 'Boat remains and maritime trade in the Persian Gulf' (Antiquity 2006).

nodes.label: Anatolian obsidian
nodes.full: Volcanic glass from the flows around Lake Van and in Cappadocia was flaked into blades and traded down the Euphrates and Tigris to villages the whole length of Mesopotamia, and on into the Gulf. Chemical fingerprinting of finished pieces lets archaeologists map the routes. Obsidian is the constant thread of the region's exchange, running unbroken from the Neolithic into the historic period.
nodes.src: Sourcing pioneered by Colin Renfrew, J. E. Dixon & J. R. Cann, 'Obsidian and Early Cultural Contact in the Near East' (1966); Mesopotamian distributions updated by Bernard Gratuze and Tristan Carter.

nodes.label: Halaf pottery as a gift
nodes.full: Fine Halaf vessels turn up far from the workshops that made them — across northern Syria, into the Levant and up into the Zagros — in quantities too small to be bulk trade. The likeliest explanation is that decorated pots moved as gifts and as part of marriage exchange between roughly equal communities, knitting the dispersed Halaf world together without any central authority to run it.
nodes.src: Distribution and exchange model in Patty Jo Watson & Steven LeBlanc, 'Girikihaciyan' (1990) and in Stuart Campbell, 'The Halaf Period in Iraq' (1992).

nodes.label: The Ubaid on the Gulf coast
nodes.full: Painted Ubaid pottery from southern Mesopotamian kilns has been found at more than sixty sites down the Arabian coast of the Gulf — from as-Sabiyah in Kuwait to Bahrain and beyond — alongside fish middens, pearl-oyster shell and the remains of reed boats. It is the first sustained sea trade in the Gulf: southern pottery and bitumen going out, fish, pearl-shell and probably date products coming back.
nodes.src: Robert Carter, 'The Neolithic origins of seafaring in the Arabian Gulf' (Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 2006); the classic statement in Joan Oates et al., 'Seafaring Merchants of Ur?' (Antiquity 1977).

nodes.label: Ubaid goods up the Euphrates
nodes.full: The northward half of the same movement carried Ubaid pottery, tripartite buildings and stamp-sealing practice up the Euphrates and across the former Halaf lands — to Tell Zeidan, to Değirmentepe on the upper river with its sealed storerooms and copper smelting, and into Anatolia. Within a few centuries the whole of Mesopotamia and its margins shared one material culture.
nodes.src: Tell Zeidan in Gil Stein's reports (2009–12); Değirmentepe in Ufuk Esin's excavations; synthesis in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010).

nodes.label: Importing stone, metal, timber and bitumen
nodes.full: The alluvium produced grain, wool, dates, fish and reeds in abundance and almost nothing else — no stone, no ore, no construction timber, no bitumen. From the beginning it drew these in: bitumen from the seeps at Hit for waterproofing and mortar, hard stone and copper from the Zagros and Anatolia, cedar and pine floated from the northern mountains. The south's later drive to control trade routes starts from this founding dependence.
nodes.src: Bitumen sourcing in Jacques Connan & Thomas Van de Velde, and in Marschner & Wright; the alluvium's resource deficit set out in Daniel Potts, 'Mesopotamian Civilization: The Material Foundations' (1997).

nodes.label: The rivers build the plain
nodes.full: The southern plain is river-made — silt dropped by the Tigris and Euphrates over a subsiding basin, laid so flat that the channels wander and jump their banks. Older accounts put the head of the Gulf far up near Ur; the revised picture keeps the coastline close to its present line but with a wide belt of shifting marsh, lagoon and levee. Settlement clung to the natural riverbanks, the only high, well-drained ground.
nodes.src: Coastline revision in Jennifer Pournelle's geoarchaeology and in Kennett & Kennett (2006); river behaviour in Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981).

nodes.label: The 8.2-kiloyear cold snap
nodes.full: Around 6200 BC the northern hemisphere suffered a sharp, roughly century-and-a-half episode of cold and drought, registered in Greenland ice cores and in Near Eastern lake and cave records. Some argue it thinned the rain-fed settlement of the steppe and pushed people toward permanently watered ground — the Samarra river valleys and the marsh-fringed south. The causal link is argued rather than proven, but the timing fits the first firm settlement of the alluvium.
nodes.src: The event defined in Alley et al. (1997); its proposed Near Eastern demographic effect in Weninger et al. (2006) and debated in Flohr et al. (2016).

nodes.label: Downhill from the hilly flanks
nodes.full: Farming and herding were first put together in the well-watered 'hilly flanks' of the Zagros and the Taurus, where the wild ancestors of wheat, barley, sheep and goat grew. The alluvium below had none of those wild resources and no stone or timber — but once irrigation unlocked its deep soil it could feed far more people. Over these millennia the region's centre of gravity moved off the hills and down onto the plain.
nodes.src: Robert Braidwood's 'hilly flanks' model from the Jarmo project (1948–55); the downhill demographic shift traced in Frank Hole's Deh Luran and Susiana surveys.

nodes.label: The marsh world
nodes.full: Where the rivers spread and slowed, a permanent wetland of reed beds, open water and shifting islands covered thousands of square kilometres. It gave fish, waterfowl, turtles, wild pig, and reed for houses, mats and boats, and it could be moved through only by water. The way of life the Ubaid marsh-dwellers led — reed house, reed boat, fishing, fowling — ran on with little change to the Marsh Arabs of the twentieth century.
nodes.src: Ecology and continuity in Edward Ochsenschlager, 'Iraq's Marsh Arabs in the Garden of Eden' (2004); Ubaid marsh exploitation in the al-Ubaid and Eridu faunal reports.

nodes.label: From hamlet to town
nodes.full: The Hassuna and Halaf north was a landscape of small villages of a few hundred people. In the Ubaid south, survey shows settlement thickening and a size hierarchy emerging, until by the end of the period Eridu, Ur, Uruk and Tepe Gawra covered ten hectares or more. That thickening is the runway; the Uruk period that follows is the take-off into the world's first cities.
nodes.src: Settlement survey data in Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981) and Adams & Nissen, 'The Uruk Countryside' (1972); northern comparison in Stuart Campbell's Halaf survey work.

nodes.label: The farming life read from bone
nodes.full: Skeletons from Samarran and Ubaid sites show the trade-offs of the settled cereal life: worn teeth from flour ground on stone querns, spinal and joint wear from grinding, digging and carrying, and the pitting of the skull that signals chronic anaemia — from marsh-borne malaria and parasites, and from a diet leaning heavily on barley. Life was not obviously longer or healthier than the foragers' before them, only more numerous.
nodes.src: Palaeopathology of the Tell es-Sawwan and Eridu remains reported in the site monographs; regional synthesis in Arkadiusz Sołtysiak's bioarchaeological work on ancient Mesopotamia.

nodes.label: The shaped head
nodes.full: A number of Ubaid skulls from Eridu and other southern sites were deliberately reshaped in infancy — bound or boarded to grow long and sloping. The same elongated head is exaggerated on the ophidian clay figurines. A modelled skull is a permanent, unmistakable mark carried for life, most likely of the group or the standing a person was born into.
nodes.src: Ubaid cranial modification analysed by Kirsi Lorentz (2010) and in the Eridu cemetery report (Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 1981); the figurine parallel noted by Karina Croucher (2012).

nodes.label: Life in the tripartite house
nodes.full: The standard Ubaid house — a long central hall with rooms ranged symmetrically on either side — framed the working day: grinding, cooking and gathering in the hall, sleeping and storing in the side rooms, ovens and bins built in. The size of the largest houses and their clusters of burials point to co-resident extended families as the unit that farmed, stored and inherited together.
nodes.src: Tell Abada household archaeology in Sabah Abboud Jasim, 'The Ubaid Period in Iraq' (1985); house-and-family analysis in Susan Pollock, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1999).

nodes.label: A shallow gradient of rank
nodes.full: Ubaid society was not flat — one house at Tell Abada is much larger and holds most of the site's child burials, some infants were buried with more goods than others, and only some people owned seals. But there are no chiefs' residences, no rich adult tombs, no monuments to individuals. The distance between the most and least advantaged was still small, and the inherited advantage only beginning to show.
nodes.src: Differential child burial at Tell Abada in Jasim (1985); the emerging-hierarchy debate in Gil Stein, 'Economy, Ritual, and Power in Ubaid Mesopotamia' (1994).

nodes.label: The tools of the day
nodes.full: Grinding stones, spindle whorls, loom weights, potter's tools, sickles, net-sinkers, hoes and digging sticks fill the settlements and the graves. Grave associations and figurines are read, cautiously, for a division of labour — women with grinding and textile work, men with herding and heavy field and canal work — but the evidence is patchy and the categories may be ours, not theirs.
nodes.src: Tool assemblages in the Yarim Tepe, Tell es-Sawwan and Tell Abada reports; the caution about projecting gender roles in Diane Bolger, 'Gender Through Time in the Ancient Near East' (2008).
